## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Large Random Matrices and Applications to Machine Learning
  Official title       Grandes matrices aléatoires application à l’apprentissage / Large Random Matrices and Application to machine learning
  Instructors          J. NAJIM, H. LEBEAU (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 30 h (lectures 24 h, labs 6 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Theory
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com course page is written in French)
  Assessment           50% lab reports (“compte-rendus TP”) and 50% final exam, a written test or a project (master-mva.com); Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment)
  Prerequisites        A course in probability (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, statistics or signal processing who wants to know why classical estimators fail when the dimension is comparable to the number of samples, and how to correct them.

**Empirical first**: draw 1000 samples of a 500-dimensional standard Gaussian vector. The true covariance is the identity, so every eigenvalue equals 1. Yet the eigenvalues of the sample covariance spread from 0.08 to 2.87, and its condition number is about 35 (code in [ch. 0](#ch0)). This spread is not bad luck: the Marchenko–Pastur law predicts it to two decimals, and it biases every method that plugs the sample covariance in.

This course studies the spectra of large random matrices when both dimensions grow at the same rate. It builds the tools (Stieltjes transform, Gaussian calculus, deterministic equivalents), proves the two founding limit theorems, and then uses them to design and analyse estimators and detectors for wireless communications, array processing, graphs and kernel methods.

It shares tools with [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html), [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html), [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html) and [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Compute and invert the Stieltjes transform of a spectral measure, and use it to prove the convergence of empirical spectral distributions.
-   Apply Gaussian integration by parts and the Poincaré–Nash inequality to compute expectations and bound variances of traces of resolvents.
-   State and prove the Marchenko–Pastur theorem for Gaussian data, and compute its support, density and moments.
-   Write the deterministic equivalents of sample covariance, variance-profile and signal-plus-noise models, and solve their fixed-point equations numerically.
-   Predict the ergodic capacity of a large multi-antenna channel and explain why it grows linearly with the number of antennas.
-   Locate the outlier eigenvalues of a spiked model, compute the alignment of its eigenvectors, and explain the phase transition.
-   Use the Tracy–Widom law to set the threshold of a test based on the largest eigenvalue.
-   Derive the generalized likelihood ratio test for source detection and predict its power in the high-dimensional regime.
-   Build consistent G-estimators of population eigenvalues and powers, and use them to locate a transmitter.
-   Correct the MUSIC algorithm for large arrays, detect communities in a dense graph, and analyse kernel spectral clustering with the same spiked-model tools.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com announces an introduction to the theory of large random matrices, and in particular to its applications to signal processing and learning. The only prerequisite it lists is a course in probability.

It states that the methodological and the applied aspects are presented separately on purpose, and that the course integrates the two. The first part covers the theory: the basic techniques, the Marchenko–Pastur and Tracy–Widom theorems, and the structured and spiked models used in statistics.

The second part lists six applications, from multi-antenna channels to kernel methods. The organisation announced is 10 sessions of 3 hours and one exam session. Assessment counts the lab reports for 50% and a final exam, a written test or a project, for 50%.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisite: a course in probability. In practice the course also uses linear algebra (spectral theorem, min-max), complex analysis at the level of holomorphic functions and residues, and Gaussian vectors; ch. 0 reviews them.

-   **Refreshers** — [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) and [Scientific Python](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) cover ch. 0 and the code.
-   **Semester 1 courses that prepare it** — [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (PCA, ridge regression, high-dimensional risk), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (Monte Carlo, used to check every limit), and [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html) (double descent, whose precise curves come from the tools of ch. 4 and ch. 14).
-   **Related courses of semester 2** — [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (kernel matrices, ch. 12), [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html) (spectral clustering, stochastic block models, ch. 11), [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html) (likelihood ratio tests, ch. 8) and [Interactions: Complexity, Stochasticity, Extrema and Rare Events](../s2-interactions/index.html) (extremes; the Tracy–Widom law of ch. 7 is the extreme-value law of a strongly correlated system).
-   **After the course** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html): high-dimensional statistics, wireless communications and the theory of learning all use these tools.

### Course outline

-   **0. Review** — eigenvalue inequalities, resolvents, Schur complements, quadratic forms of random vectors.
-   **1. Spectral measures and the Stieltjes transform** — the transform, its inversion, the continuity theorem, rank perturbations.
-   **2. Gaussian matrix calculus and the Poincaré–Nash inequality** — integration by parts, variance bounds, the semicircle law as a first application.
-   **3. The Marchenko–Pastur theorem** — the limit spectrum of a sample covariance matrix, its edges and moments.
-   **4. Structured models and deterministic equivalents** — population covariance, variance profile, signal plus noise.
-   **5. MIMO channels** — mutual information and ergodic capacity of large multi-antenna channels.
-   **6. Spiked models** — outlier eigenvalues, eigenvector alignment and the phase transition.
-   **7. The largest eigenvalue and the Tracy–Widom law** — fluctuations at the edge and how to compute the law.
-   **8. Source detection and spectrum sensing** — the generalized likelihood ratio test and its limits.
-   **9. G-estimation, power estimation and positioning** — consistent estimators of population quantities, applied to locating a transmitter.
-   **10. Array processing** — MUSIC, its failure with large arrays, and the G-MUSIC correction.
-   **11. Community detection on large graphs** — the spectral detectability threshold of the stochastic block model.
-   **12. Kernel random matrices** — why kernel matrices linearize in high dimension, and what it implies for kernel spectral clustering.
-   **13. Complements for self-study** — general entries, the moment method, free probability, fluctuations, shrinkage.
-   **14. Research directions and open problems** — a self-study tour of current work.

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1 if the min-max theorem or Schur complements feel distant: the proofs use them without warning.
-   After each session, do the exercises of its row, then run the code of the chapter and change one parameter (the ratio of dimensions, the spike strength, the sample size) to see the limit appear.
-   Check every limit theorem by simulation before trusting it at finite size: the code blocks show how close the asymptotic formulas already are for matrices of size 50 to 1000.
-   The code uses NumPy and SciPy only, with synthetic data; every block runs in a few seconds on a laptop.
-   The lab slots of sessions 3, 5, 8 and 10 use the code of chapters 1–3, 5, 8–9 and 10–12; the projects of the last section extend them.

## 0. Review: eigenvalues, resolvents and Gaussian vectors {#ch0}

Every chapter manipulates the eigenvalues of large Hermitian matrices through their resolvents, and averages quadratic forms of random vectors. This chapter collects the M1-level facts used later, with short proofs.

The [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization refresher](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) and the [Probability and Statistics refresher](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) cover the same ground at a slower pace.

The phenomenon that motivates the course takes five lines of NumPy: white data, a sample covariance, and eigenvalues that are far from 1.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, n = 500, 1000                      # dimension, number of samples
X = rng.standard_normal((N, n))       # white data: true covariance = I
S = X @ X.T / n                       # sample covariance
lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(S)
c = N / n
print(f"smallest / largest eigenvalue: {lam.min():.3f} / {lam.max():.3f}")
print(f"Marchenko-Pastur edges       : {(1 - c**0.5)**2:.3f} / {(1 + c**0.5)**2:.3f}")
print(f"condition number of S        : {lam.max() / lam.min():.1f}")
```

The output gives eigenvalues between 0.082 and 2.868, against the predicted edges 0.086 and 2.914 of ch. 3, and a condition number of 34.9 instead of 1.

### Eigenvalue inequalities

Throughout, $A$ and $B$ are Hermitian $N \times N$ matrices, with eigenvalues in decreasing order $\lambda_1(A) \geq \dots \geq \lambda_N(A)$. The spectral norm is $\|A\| = \max_k |\lambda_k(A)|$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — Courant–Fischer min-max]{.tag} For every $k$,
$$
\lambda_k(A) = \max_{\dim V = k}\; \min_{x \in V,\, \|x\| = 1} x^* A x .
$$

::: proof
Let $(e_i)$ be an orthonormal eigenbasis. On $V_0 = \mathrm{span}(e_1, \dots, e_k)$, every unit $x$ has $x^* A x \geq \lambda_k$, so the maximum is at least $\lambda_k$.

Conversely, any $V$ of dimension $k$ meets $\mathrm{span}(e_k, \dots, e_N)$, of dimension $N - k + 1$, in a non-zero vector. On that vector $x^* A x \leq \lambda_k \|x\|^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Weyl and interlacing inequalities]{.tag} (a) Weyl: for every $k$,
$$
|\lambda_k(A) - \lambda_k(B)| \leq \|A - B\| .
$$

*(b)* Interlacing: if $\mathrm{rank}(A - B) \leq r$, then, for every $k \leq N - r$ and symmetrically in $A$ and $B$,
$$
\lambda_{k + r}(A) \leq \lambda_k(B) .
$$
The numbers of eigenvalues of $A$ and of $B$ above any level $t$ differ by at most $r$.

::: proof
*(a)* $x^* A x \leq x^* B x + \|A - B\|$ for unit $x$; take the max-min of Theorem 0.1 on both sides, then exchange $A$ and $B$.

*(b)* Let $V$ realize $\lambda_{k+r}(A)$ in Theorem 0.1. The space $V' = V \cap \ker(A - B)$ has dimension at least $k$, and $A = B$ on it. Hence
$$
\lambda_{k+r}(A) \leq \min_{x \in V',\, \|x\| = 1} x^* B x \leq \lambda_k(B) .
$$
The counting statement follows. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Resolvents, Sherman–Morrison and Schur complements

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Resolvent]{.tag} The resolvent of $A$ at $z \in \mathbb{C}$ outside its spectrum is
$$
Q_A(z) = (A - z I_N)^{-1} .
$$
We write $\mathbb{C}^+ = \{z : \Im z > 0\}$ and, for $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$, $v = \Im z$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Resolvent toolbox]{.tag} For $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$:

1.  $\|Q_A(z)\| \leq 1 / v$, and more generally $\|Q_A(z)\| = 1/\mathrm{dist}(z, \mathrm{spec}\, A)$.
2.  Resolvent identity: $Q_A - Q_B = Q_A (B - A) Q_B$, and $\frac{d}{dz} Q_A = Q_A^2$.
3.  Sherman–Morrison: for invertible $M$ and vectors $u, w$ with $1 + w^* M^{-1} u \neq 0$,
    $$
    (M + u w^*)^{-1} u = \frac{M^{-1} u}{1 + w^* M^{-1} u} .
    $$
4.  Determinant lemma: $\det(M + u w^*) = \det(M)\,(1 + w^* M^{-1} u)$.

::: proof
*(1)* $Q_A$ is normal with eigenvalues $1/(\lambda_k - z)$, of modulus at most $1/v$. (2) Multiply $(A - z)^{-1}$ on the left and $(B - z)^{-1}$ on the right of $(B - z) - (A - z)$.

*(3)* Multiply both sides by $M + u w^*$. (4) Factor out $M$: $\det(I + M^{-1} u w^*) = 1 + w^* M^{-1} u$, since $M^{-1} u w^*$ has rank one. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Schur complement formula inverts a matrix by blocks: if $M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b^* \\ b & D \end{pmatrix}$ with $a$ scalar and $D$ invertible, the top-left entry of the inverse is
$$
(M^{-1})_{11} = \frac{1}{a - b^* D^{-1} b} .
$$
It gives the diagonal entries of a resolvent in terms of the resolvent of a smaller matrix, which is the starting point of the general-entries proofs of ch. 13.

### Quadratic forms of random vectors

The workhorse of the course is the concentration of $x^* A x$ around $\mathrm{tr}\, A$ when $x$ has independent standardized entries and $A$ is independent of $x$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Trace lemma]{.tag} Let $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_N)$ and $A$ a deterministic real symmetric matrix. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\, x^\top A x = \mathrm{tr}\, A, \qquad \mathrm{Var}\,(x^\top A x) = 2\, \mathrm{tr}\, A^2 \leq 2 N \|A\|^2 .
$$
Hence the normalized form satisfies
$$
\frac{1}{N} x^\top A x - \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, A = O_P\big(\|A\| N^{-1/2}\big) .
$$

::: proof
Write $A = O D O^\top$ with $O$ orthogonal. The vector $g = O^\top x$ is again standard Gaussian, and $x^\top A x = \sum_k d_k g_k^2$. The $g_k^2$ are independent with mean 1 and variance 2. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For independent entries with mean 0, variance 1 and finite fourth moment, and complex $A$, the same bound holds up to a constant (Bai and Silverstein, 2010, Lemma B.26):
$$
\mathbb{E}\, |x^* A x - \mathrm{tr}\, A|^2 \leq C\, \mathrm{tr}(A A^*) .
$$
::::

::: note
[Probability reminders]{.tag} A sequence of probability measures $\mu_N$ converges **weakly** to $\mu$ when $\int f\, d\mu_N \to \int f\, d\mu$ for every bounded continuous $f$.

Borel–Cantelli: if $\sum_N \mathbb{P}(|Y_N| > \varepsilon) < \infty$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, then $Y_N \to 0$ almost surely. With Chebyshev's inequality, a variance of order $N^{-2}$ is enough.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Weyl: eigenvalues move by at most the norm of the perturbation. Interlacing: a rank-$r$ perturbation moves the eigenvalue counts by at most $r$.
-   The resolvent is bounded by $1/\Im z$ off the real axis. Sherman–Morrison and the determinant lemma handle rank-one updates.
-   A quadratic form $x^* A x$ concentrates around $\mathrm{tr}\, A$ at relative order $N^{-1/2}$.
:::

## 1. Spectral measures and the Stieltjes transform {#ch1}

The object of the course is the distribution of the eigenvalues of a large matrix. The Stieltjes transform turns it into an analytic function that equals the normalized trace of the resolvent, and that is what the proofs compute.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Empirical spectral distribution]{.tag} The empirical spectral distribution (ESD) of a Hermitian $N \times N$ matrix $A$ and its distribution function are
$$
\mu_A = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \delta_{\lambda_k(A)}, \qquad F^A(t) = \frac{1}{N}\, \#\{k : \lambda_k(A) \leq t\} .
$$
When $A$ is random, $\mu_A$ is a random probability measure.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Stieltjes transform]{.tag} The Stieltjes transform of a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is the function on $\mathbb{C}^+$
$$
m_\mu(z) = \int \frac{\mu(d\lambda)}{\lambda - z} .
$$
For an ESD it is a normalized trace of the resolvent:
$$
m_{\mu_A}(z) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{1}{\lambda_k(A) - z} = \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, Q_A(z) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Basic properties]{.tag} Let $m = m_\mu$ and $z = x + iv \in \mathbb{C}^+$.

1.  $m$ is analytic on $\mathbb{C}^+$ and $\Im m(z) > 0$.
2.  $|m(z)| \leq 1/v$.
3.  $-iy\, m(iy) \to 1$ as $y \to +\infty$.
4.  If $\mu$ is carried by $[0, \infty)$, then $\Im\big(z\, m(z)\big) \geq 0$.

::: proof
*(1)* Differentiate under the integral; the imaginary part of $1/(\lambda - z)$ is $v/|\lambda - z|^2 > 0$. (2) $|\lambda - z| \geq v$.

*(3)* $-iy/(\lambda - iy) \to 1$ pointwise, with modulus at most 1: dominated convergence.

*(4)* The imaginary part of $z/(\lambda - z)$ equals $\lambda v / |\lambda - z|^2 \geq 0$ when $\lambda \geq 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Conversely, an analytic map from $\mathbb{C}^+$ to $\mathbb{C}^+$ with property 3 is the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure (Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, 2010, §2.4). This is how a solution of a fixed-point equation is recognized as a Stieltjes transform.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Inversion formula]{.tag} If $a < b$ are not atoms of $\mu$, then
$$
\mu\big((a, b)\big) = \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\pi} \int_a^b \Im\, m_\mu(x + i\varepsilon)\, dx .
$$
If $\mu$ has a density $f$ continuous at $x$, then
$$
f(x) = \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\pi} \Im\, m_\mu(x + i\varepsilon) .
$$

::: proof
The imaginary part is a convolution with the Cauchy density $P_\varepsilon$ of scale $\varepsilon$:
$$
\frac{1}{\pi} \Im\, m_\mu(x + i\varepsilon) = \int \frac{1}{\pi} \frac{\varepsilon}{(\lambda - x)^2 + \varepsilon^2}\, \mu(d\lambda) = (P_\varepsilon * \mu)(x) .
$$

By Fubini, the integral over $(a, b)$ equals
$$
\int \frac{1}{\pi} \Big[ \arctan \frac{b - \lambda}{\varepsilon} - \arctan \frac{a - \lambda}{\varepsilon} \Big]\, \mu(d\lambda) .
$$

The integrand is bounded by 1 and tends to 1 on $(a, b)$, to $1/2$ at $a$ and $b$, and to 0 outside $[a, b]$.

Dominated convergence and $\mu(\{a\}) = \mu(\{b\}) = 0$ give the first claim. The second is the convergence of $P_\varepsilon * \mu$ at a continuity point of the density. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Continuity theorem]{.tag} Let $\mu_N$ and $\mu$ be probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$. Then $\mu_N \to \mu$ weakly if and only if $m_{\mu_N}(z) \to m_\mu(z)$ for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$.

It suffices that the convergence holds on a countable set with an accumulation point in $\mathbb{C}^+$. For random measures, convergence almost surely on such a set implies weak convergence almost surely.

::: proof
($\Rightarrow$) For fixed $z$, $\lambda \mapsto 1/(\lambda - z)$ is bounded and continuous.

($\Leftarrow$) By Helly's selection theorem, every subsequence has a further subsequence converging vaguely to a sub-probability measure $\nu$. The function $1/(\lambda - z)$ vanishes at infinity, so $m_\nu = m_\mu$ on the countable set. Both are analytic on $\mathbb{C}^+$, so they agree everywhere by the identity theorem.

Theorem 1.4 then gives $\nu = \mu$. As $\mu$ has mass 1, no mass escapes, the convergence is weak, and the limit does not depend on the subsequence. For random measures, apply this on the event of probability one where the countable convergence holds. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Stieltjes transform also controls finite-rank perturbations, which is the first hint of the spiked models of ch. 6.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.6 — Rank perturbations do not move the ESD]{.tag} If $\mathrm{rank}(A - B) \leq r$, then
$$
\sup_t |F^A(t) - F^B(t)| \leq \frac{r}{N}, \qquad |m_{\mu_A}(z) - m_{\mu_B}(z)| \leq \frac{\pi r}{N v} .
$$

::: proof
The first bound is the counting statement of Proposition 0.2. For the second, integrate by parts:
$$
m_{\mu_A}(z) - m_{\mu_B}(z) = \int \frac{d(F^A - F^B)(t)}{t - z} = \int \frac{F^A(t) - F^B(t)}{(t - z)^2}\, dt .
$$
Its modulus is at most
$$
\frac{r}{N} \int \frac{dt}{(t - x)^2 + v^2} = \frac{\pi r}{N v} .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

So the ESD cannot see a perturbation of fixed rank. Centring the data, for instance, subtracts a rank-one matrix from the sample covariance and does not change its limit (Exercise 2). Individual eigenvalues, however, can move far away: that is the subject of ch. 6.

::: ex
[Example 1.7 — Two atoms]{.tag} For $A = \mathrm{diag}(1, 3)$,
$$
m_{\mu_A}(z) = \frac{1}{2} \Big( \frac{1}{1 - z} + \frac{1}{3 - z} \Big) .
$$
At $z = 2 + 0.1 i$, this gives $m = 0.099\, i$: the real parts cancel at the midpoint, and $\frac{1}{\pi}\Im\, m = 0.03$ says that there is little mass near 2.

At $z = 1 + 0.1 i$, $\frac{1}{\pi}\Im\, m = 1.60$. This is a Cauchy bump of height $\frac{1}{2\pi\varepsilon} \approx 1.59$ above the atom at 1, which carries mass $1/2$, plus 0.004 from the atom at 3.

As $\varepsilon \to 0$ the bump concentrates on the atom, as Theorem 1.4 says.
:::

The code recovers the density of a sample covariance spectrum from its Stieltjes transform, at three values of $\varepsilon$:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
N, n = 400, 1600
c = N / n
X = rng.standard_normal((N, n))
lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X @ X.T / n)

def stieltjes(z):                     # m_N(z) = (1/N) tr (S - z I)^{-1}
    return np.mean(1.0 / (lam - z))

a, b = (1 - c**0.5) ** 2, (1 + c**0.5) ** 2
def mp_density(x):
    return np.sqrt(max((b - x) * (x - a), 0.0)) / (2 * np.pi * c * x)

print("x     eps=0.1  eps=0.03  eps=0.01  MP density")
for x in [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0]:
    approx = [stieltjes(x + 1j * eps).imag / np.pi for eps in (0.1, 0.03, 0.01)]
    print(f"{x:<5} " + "  ".join(f"{v:7.3f}" for v in approx) + f"  {mp_density(x):9.3f}")
```

With $\varepsilon = 0.1$ the estimate is smoothed (0.669 against 0.842 at $x = 0.5$, near the left edge). With $\varepsilon = 0.01$, close to the eigenvalue spacing, it starts to follow individual eigenvalues (0.231 against 0.211 at $x = 2$). The useful range is between the spacing $1/N$ and the scale of the density.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   The Stieltjes transform of an ESD is $\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, Q(z)$: spectra become traces of resolvents.
-   Inversion: the density is $\frac{1}{\pi} \Im\, m(x + i0)$. Continuity: weak convergence is pointwise convergence of $m$ on $\mathbb{C}^+$.
-   A rank-$r$ perturbation changes the ESD by at most $r/N$: limit spectra ignore low-rank signals, individual eigenvalues do not.
:::

## 2. Gaussian matrix calculus and the Poincaré–Nash inequality {#ch2}

For matrices with Gaussian entries, two tools replace most of the combinatorics of random matrix theory: integration by parts computes expectations of traces of resolvents, and the Poincaré–Nash inequality shows that their variance is negligible. This approach goes back to Pastur, and Hachem, Loubaton, Najim and coauthors used it systematically for wireless channels.

### Integration by parts and the Poincaré–Nash inequality

:::: prop
[Lemma 2.1 — Gaussian integration by parts]{.tag} Let $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Gamma)$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{C}$ of class $C^1$.

If $f$ and $\nabla f$ have polynomial growth, then, for every $i$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[x_i\, f(x)\big] = \sum_{j=1}^d \Gamma_{ij}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\partial_j f(x)\big] .
$$

::: proof
For $d = 1$ and $\Gamma = 1$, the standard density $\varphi$ satisfies $\varphi'(t) = -t \varphi(t)$, so an integration by parts gives
$$
\int t f(t) \varphi(t)\, dt = -\int f(t) \varphi'(t)\, dt = \int f'(t) \varphi(t)\, dt .
$$
For independent standard coordinates, apply this to one coordinate with the others fixed. In general write $x = \Gamma^{1/2} g$ with $g$ standard and use the chain rule. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For a complex Gaussian $z \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, 1)$ the same computation gives $\mathbb{E}[z f] = \mathbb{E}[\partial f / \partial \bar z]$, which is the form used for complex channels.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Poincaré–Nash inequality]{.tag} With $x$ and $f$ as in Lemma 2.1 and $f$ real,
$$
\mathrm{Var}\, f(x) \leq \mathbb{E}\big[ \nabla f(x)^\top\, \Gamma\, \nabla f(x) \big] .
$$
For complex $f$, applying it to $\Re f$ and $\Im f$ gives
$$
\mathbb{E}\, |f(x) - \mathbb{E} f(x)|^2 \leq \mathbb{E}\big[ \overline{\nabla f(x)}^\top\, \Gamma\, \nabla f(x) \big] .
$$

::: proof
By the change of variables $x = \Gamma^{1/2} g$, assume $\Gamma = I$. Let $y$ be an independent copy of $x$, and for $t \in [0, 1]$ let
$$
Z_t = \sqrt{t}\, x + \sqrt{1 - t}\, y, \qquad \phi(t) = \mathbb{E}\big[f(x)\, f(Z_t)\big] .
$$

-   Endpoints: $Z_1 = x$ and $Z_0 = y$ is independent of $x$, so $\phi(1) - \phi(0) = \mathrm{Var}\, f(x)$.
-   Derivative: by the chain rule,
    $$
    \phi'(t) = \mathbb{E}\Big[f(x)\, \nabla f(Z_t) \cdot \Big(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{t}} - \frac{y}{2\sqrt{1-t}}\Big)\Big] .
    $$
-   Lemma 2.1 in $y$ gives
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[f(x)\, \partial_i f(Z_t)\, y_i\big] = \sqrt{1 - t}\; \mathbb{E}\big[f(x)\, \partial_{ii} f(Z_t)\big] .
    $$
-   Lemma 2.1 in $x$ gives
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[f(x)\, \partial_i f(Z_t)\, x_i\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\partial_i f(x)\, \partial_i f(Z_t)\big] + \sqrt{t}\; \mathbb{E}\big[f(x)\, \partial_{ii} f(Z_t)\big] .
    $$

The second-derivative terms cancel, which leaves
$$
\phi'(t) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla f(x) \cdot \nabla f(Z_t)\big] .
$$

Since $Z_t$ has the same law as $x$, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the expectation by $\mathbb{E} |\nabla f(x)|^2$. Integrating, $\int_0^1 \frac{dt}{2\sqrt{t}} = 1$ gives the claim. Functions that are only $C^1$ are handled by smoothing. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Derivatives of resolvents

In the rest of the chapter and in ch. 3, $X$ is an $N \times n$ matrix with independent $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ entries and columns $x_1, \dots, x_n$. We set
$$
\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X X^\top, \qquad Q(z) = (\Sigma - z I_N)^{-1}, \qquad m_N(z) = \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, Q(z) .
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Derivatives of the resolvent]{.tag} Let $e_i$ be the $i$-th canonical vector of $\mathbb{R}^N$. Then
$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial X_{ij}} = -\frac{1}{n}\, Q \big(e_i x_j^\top + x_j e_i^\top\big) Q, \qquad \frac{\partial\, \mathrm{tr}\, Q}{\partial X_{ij}} = -\frac{2}{n}\, \big(Q^2 X\big)_{ij} .
$$

::: proof
Differentiate $Q (\Sigma - z) = I$: $\partial Q = -Q\, (\partial \Sigma)\, Q$, and
$$
\frac{\partial \Sigma}{\partial X_{ij}} = \frac{1}{n}\big(e_i x_j^\top + x_j e_i^\top\big) .
$$
For the trace, use $\mathrm{tr}(Q A Q) = \mathrm{tr}(Q^2 A)$ and the symmetry $Q^\top = Q$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — The trace of the resolvent barely fluctuates]{.tag} For $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$ with $v = \Im z$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\, |m_N(z) - \mathbb{E}\, m_N(z)|^2 \leq \frac{4}{N n v^4} .
$$
Consequently, if $N/n \to c > 0$, then $m_N(z) - \mathbb{E}\, m_N(z) \to 0$ almost surely, for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$.

::: proof
By Proposition 2.3 and $\|Q\| \leq 1/v$,
$$
\sum_{i,j} \Big| \frac{\partial m_N}{\partial X_{ij}} \Big|^2 = \frac{4}{N^2 n^2}\, \|Q^2 X\|_F^2 \leq \frac{4}{N^2 n^2 v^4}\, \|X\|_F^2 .
$$
Theorem 2.2 with $\mathbb{E} \|X\|_F^2 = N n$ gives the bound. It is of order $N^{-2}$, which is summable: Chebyshev and Borel–Cantelli give the almost sure convergence. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The variance is of order $N^{-2}$, not $N^{-1}$: $\mathrm{tr}\, Q$ is a sum of $N$ terms but fluctuates by $O(1)$ only. This rigidity of spectra is quantified by the central limit theorem of ch. 13.

### First application: the semicircle law

A Wigner matrix is the simplest model. Wigner (1955, 1958) found its limit law by the moment method (ch. 13); the Gaussian method proves it in a few lines.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — Semicircle law for the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble]{.tag} Let $G$ be $N \times N$ with independent $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ entries and $W = (G + G^\top)/\sqrt{2N}$. Almost surely, $\mu_W$ converges weakly to the semicircle law
$$
\sigma(dx) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{4 - x^2}\; \mathbf{1}_{[-2, 2]}(x)\, dx ,
$$
whose Stieltjes transform is the root with positive imaginary part of $m^2 + z m + 1 = 0$:
$$
m_{\mathrm{sc}}(z) = \frac{-z + \sqrt{z^2 - 4}}{2} .
$$
The branch of the square root behaves like $z$ at infinity.

::: proof
Let $Q = (W - z)^{-1}$ and $m_N = \frac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}\, Q$.

1.  *Resolvent identity.* $W Q = I + z Q$, so that
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\, \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}(W Q) = 1 + z\, \mathbb{E}\, m_N .
    $$
2.  *Integration by parts.* $W$ is linear in $G$, so Lemma 2.1 in the variables $G_{ab}$, with $\partial Q = -Q\, (\partial W)\, Q$, gives for all $i, j$
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[W_{ij} Q_{ji}\big] = -\frac{1}{N}\, \mathbb{E}\big[Q_{ji}^2 + Q_{ii} Q_{jj}\big] .
    $$
3.  *Summation.* Summing over $i, j$ and dividing by $N$:
    $$
    1 + z\, \mathbb{E}\, m_N = -\mathbb{E}\, m_N^2 - \frac{1}{N^2}\, \mathbb{E}\, \mathrm{tr}\, Q^2 .
    $$
4.  *Closing the equation.* The last term is at most $1/(N v^2)$. Theorem 2.2 gives a variance of order $N^{-2}$ (Exercise 9), so $\mathbb{E}\, m_N^2 = (\mathbb{E}\, m_N)^2 + O(N^{-2})$, and
    $$
    (\mathbb{E}\, m_N)^2 + z\, \mathbb{E}\, m_N + 1 = O\big(N^{-1}\big) .
    $$
5.  *Identification.* The functions $\mathbb{E}\, m_N$ are analytic and bounded by $1/v$, so by Montel's theorem every subsequence has a further subsequence converging locally uniformly on $\mathbb{C}^+$ to an analytic $m$. This limit solves $m^2 + zm + 1 = 0$ and $\Im m \geq 0$.
6.  *The right root.* The two roots have product 1, so their imaginary parts have opposite signs, and neither is real. Exactly one root lies in $\mathbb{C}^+$, so $m = m_{\mathrm{sc}}$, and the whole sequence converges.
7.  *Conclusion.* Proposition 2.4 (in its Wigner form) and Theorem 1.5 give the almost sure weak convergence; Theorem 1.4 turns $m_{\mathrm{sc}}$ into the density, since $\Im \sqrt{x^2 - 4} = \sqrt{4 - x^2}$ on $(-2, 2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.6 — The golden ratio]{.tag} At $z = i$, $z^2 - 4 = -5$ and the branch gives $\sqrt{z^2 - 4} = i\sqrt{5}$. Hence
$$
m_{\mathrm{sc}}(i) = \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}\, i \approx 0.618\, i .
$$
Directly, $\Im\, m_{\mathrm{sc}}(i)$ is the average of $1/(1 + x^2)$ under the semicircle law, since $\Im \frac{1}{x - i} = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$.
:::

The code checks the two orders of magnitude of the proof: the bias of $\mathbb{E}\, m_N$ is of order $1/N$ and the variance of order $1/N^2$.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

def goe(N):
    G = rng.standard_normal((N, N))
    return (G + G.T) / np.sqrt(2 * N)          # off-diagonal variance 1/N

z = 1.0 + 0.5j
m_sc = (-z + np.sqrt(z - 2) * np.sqrt(z + 2)) / 2   # branch with Im m > 0
print(f"semicircle m(z) = {m_sc:.4f}")
for N in [50, 100, 200, 400]:
    ms = np.array([np.mean(1 / (np.linalg.eigvalsh(goe(N)) - z)) for _ in range(200)])
    print(f"N={N:3d}: mean m_N = {ms.mean():.4f}, "
          f"|bias| = {abs(ms.mean() - m_sc):.1e}, N^2 Var = {N**2 * ms.var():.3f}")
```

The bias falls from $3.9 \times 10^{-3}$ to $3.2 \times 10^{-4}$ as $N$ goes from 50 to 400, and $N^2\, \mathrm{Var}\, m_N$ stays near 1.7.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Integration by parts moves $x_i$ onto a derivative of $f$. With $\partial Q = -Q\, (\partial A)\, Q$, it turns $\mathbb{E}\, \mathrm{tr}(A Q)$ into products of traces.
-   Poincaré–Nash bounds $\mathrm{Var} f$ by $\mathbb{E}\, \nabla f^\top \Gamma \nabla f$. For $\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}\, Q$ it gives $O(N^{-2})$, hence almost sure convergence.
-   The scheme: identity, integration by parts, variance bound, limit equation, choice of the root. It gives the semicircle law here and the Marchenko–Pastur law in ch. 3.
:::

## 3. The Marchenko–Pastur theorem {#ch3}

The sample covariance matrix is the basic object of multivariate statistics. When the dimension $N$ and the sample size $n$ grow together, its spectrum does not concentrate at the population eigenvalues: it spreads over an interval whose shape the Marchenko–Pastur theorem gives.

### Statement

The data are $n$ independent vectors $x_1, \dots, x_n$ of $\mathbb{R}^N$ with independent entries of mean 0 and variance 1, so that the population covariance is $I_N$.

As in ch. 2, $X = [x_1, \dots, x_n]$ and $\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X X^\top$. We write $c_n = N/n$ and assume
$$
N, n \to \infty, \qquad c_n \to c \in (0, \infty) .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — Marchenko–Pastur (1967)]{.tag} Almost surely, $\mu_\Sigma$ converges weakly to the Marchenko–Pastur law $\mu_c$, whose Stieltjes transform $m_c$ is, for each $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$, the unique solution in $\mathbb{C}^+$ of
$$
c z\, m^2 + (z - 1 + c)\, m + 1 = 0 .
$$
Equivalently, $m = 1/(1 - c - z - c z m)$.

::: proof
We prove it for Gaussian entries; ch. 13 gives the general argument. Let $Q = (\Sigma - z)^{-1}$, $m_N = \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, Q$ and $\bar m_N = \mathbb{E}\, m_N$.

1.  *Identity.* $Q \Sigma = I + z Q$, so $\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}(Q \Sigma) = 1 + z\, m_N$.
2.  *Integration by parts.* $(Q\Sigma)_{ii} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_j (Q X)_{ij} X_{ij}$. Lemma 2.1 and Proposition 2.3 give
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[X_{ij} (QX)_{ij}\big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[ Q_{ii} - \frac{1}{n} Q_{ii}\, x_j^\top Q x_j - \frac{1}{n} (Q x_j)_i^2 \Big] .
    $$
3.  *Averaging.* Sum over $j$, divide by $n$, then average over $i$. Using $\frac{1}{n} \sum_j x_j^\top Q x_j = \mathrm{tr}(Q \Sigma)$:
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\, \tfrac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}(Q\Sigma) = \bar m_N - c_n\, \mathbb{E}\big[m_N\, \tfrac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}(Q\Sigma)\big] - \tfrac{1}{n}\, \mathbb{E}\, \tfrac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}(Q \Sigma Q) .
    $$
4.  *Closing.* Insert step 1. The last term is $O(1/n)$, because $Q \Sigma Q = Q + z Q^2$ has norm at most $1/v + |z|/v^2$. Proposition 2.4 replaces $\mathbb{E}\, m_N^2$ by $\bar m_N^2$ up to $O(n^{-2})$:
    $$
    c_n z\, \bar m_N^2 + (z - 1 + c_n)\, \bar m_N + 1 = O\big(n^{-1}\big) .
    $$
5.  *Identification.* By Montel's theorem, every limit point $m$ of $\bar m_N$ is analytic, solves the limit equation, and satisfies $\Im m \geq 0$ and $|m| \leq 1/v$.
6.  *Uniqueness.* Two distinct solutions $m_1, m_2$ of the equation $m = 1/(1 - c - z - czm)$ satisfy $c z\, m_1 m_2 = 1$.

    On $z = iy$ with $y > c$, the bound $|m_k| \leq 1/y$ gives $|c z\, m_1 m_2| \leq c/y < 1$. So the limit point is unique there, and everywhere by analyticity.
7.  *Conclusion.* $\bar m_N \to m_c$, Proposition 2.4 transfers the convergence to $m_N$ almost surely, and Theorem 1.5 concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key formula — the Marchenko–Pastur equation]{.tag}
$$
m_c(z) = \frac{1}{1 - c - z - c z\, m_c(z)}
$$
:::

### The law itself

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Density, edges and moments]{.tag} Let $a = (1 - \sqrt{c})^2$ and $b = (1 + \sqrt{c})^2$. Then
$$
\mu_c(dx) = \Big(1 - \frac{1}{c}\Big)^+ \delta_0 + \frac{\sqrt{(b - x)(x - a)}}{2\pi c\, x}\, \mathbf{1}_{[a, b]}(x)\, dx .
$$
Its mean is 1 and its second moment is $1 + c$. More generally, its $k$-th moment is a Narayana polynomial:
$$
\int x^k\, \mu_c(dx) = \sum_{r=0}^{k-1} \frac{1}{r + 1} \binom{k}{r} \binom{k - 1}{r}\, c^r .
$$

::: proof
The root with positive imaginary part is
$$
m_c(z) = \frac{1 - c - z + \sqrt{(z - 1 - c)^2 - 4c}}{2 c z} ,
$$
with the branch that makes $m_c(z) \sim -1/z$ at infinity. Note that $(z - 1 - c)^2 - 4c = (z - a)(z - b)$.

-   *Density.* For $x \in (a, b)$, $(x - a)(x - b) < 0$, and $\frac{1}{\pi} \Im\, m_c(x + i0)$ is the announced density (Theorem 1.4).
-   *Atom.* At $z \to 0$, $z\, m_c(z) \to -(1 - 1/c)^+$, which is minus the mass at 0. When $c > 1$, $\Sigma$ has rank $n < N$ and $N - n$ zero eigenvalues.
-   *Moments.* For large $|z|$, $m_c(z) = -\sum_k z^{-k-1} \int x^k d\mu_c$. Inserting this series into the equation gives a recursion for the moments, whose solution is the Narayana formula. The moment method of ch. 13 gives a combinatorial proof. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The bulk is not centred at 1 in a symmetric way: the density is larger on the left, and for $c > 1$ a fraction $1 - 1/c$ of the eigenvalues is exactly 0. The data-dependent spread has a simple first consequence: $\Sigma$ is badly conditioned even when the population covariance is the identity.

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — Numbers for c = 0.5]{.tag} With $N = 500$ and $n = 1000$:

-   edges $a = (1 - 0.707)^2 = 0.086$ and $b = (1 + 0.707)^2 = 2.914$;
-   density at $x = 1$: $(b - 1)(1 - a) = 1.914 \times 0.914 = 1.749$, so the density is $\sqrt{1.749}/\pi = 0.421$;
-   asymptotic condition number $b/a = 34.0$, against 34.9 in the simulation of ch. 0;
-   second moment $1 + c = 1.5$: the average squared eigenvalue exceeds the squared average by $c$.
:::

### Extreme eigenvalues

Weak convergence says nothing about a vanishing fraction of eigenvalues. A separate theorem controls the extreme ones, and ch. 6 and ch. 7 rely on it.

::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — No eigenvalue outside the bulk]{.tag} If the entries are independent with mean 0, variance 1 and finite fourth moment, then almost surely
$$
\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma) \to (1 + \sqrt{c})^2 ,
$$
and, if $c < 1$, $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma) \to (1 - \sqrt{c})^2$.

The first statement is due to Geman (1980) under stronger moment conditions and to Yin, Bai and Krishnaiah (1988); the second to Bai and Yin (1993). The proofs use the moment method with moments of order $k \sim \log N$, as in ch. 13. Bai and Silverstein (1998) extend it: no eigenvalue lies outside the support of the limit law of ch. 4.
:::

Ch. 13 shows how the finite fourth moment enters, and why without it the largest eigenvalue can escape to infinity while the ESD still converges.

The code checks the law, its first two moments and its universality: Gaussian and $\pm 1$ entries give the same limit.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def mp_cdf_factory(c):
    a, b = (1 - c**0.5) ** 2, (1 + c**0.5) ** 2
    dens = lambda x: np.sqrt(max((b - x) * (x - a), 0)) / (2 * np.pi * c * x)
    atom = max(1 - 1 / c, 0)
    def cdf(x):
        if x < a:
            return atom if x >= 0 else 0.0
        return atom + quad(dens, a, min(x, b))[0]
    return cdf

for N, n in [(300, 1200), (600, 1200), (1200, 600)]:
    c = N / n
    X = rng.standard_normal((N, n))            # Gaussian entries
    B = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(N, n))   # Rademacher entries
    cdf = mp_cdf_factory(c)
    for name, Z in [("gauss", X), ("rademacher", B)]:
        lam = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(Z @ Z.T / n))
        grid = np.linspace(1e-9, (1 + c**0.5) ** 2 + 0.2, 200)
        emp = np.searchsorted(lam, grid, side="right") / N
        ks = max(abs(e - cdf(g)) for e, g in zip(emp, grid))
        print(f"c={c:.2f} {name:10s}: mean {lam.mean():.3f} (1), "
              f"2nd moment {np.mean(lam**2):.3f} ({1 + c:.2f}), sup|F_N - F| = {ks:.3f}")
```

In all six cases the Kolmogorov distance to $\mu_c$ is below 0.01, and the second moments match $1 + c$ within 0.005, including $c = 2$ with its atom at 0.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   For white data with $N/n \to c$, the ESD of the sample covariance tends to $\mu_c$, carried by $[(1 - \sqrt{c})^2, (1 + \sqrt{c})^2]$, plus an atom at 0 when $c > 1$.
-   Its Stieltjes transform solves $c z m^2 + (z - 1 + c) m + 1 = 0$; the Gaussian proof is integration by parts plus a variance bound.
-   The extreme eigenvalues converge to the edges under a fourth moment, so the sample covariance is ill-conditioned even for white data.
:::

## 4. Structured models and deterministic equivalents {#ch4}

Real data are not white. This chapter treats the three structured models of the official syllabus: a population covariance matrix, a variance profile, and a deterministic signal plus noise. In each case the limit spectrum is described by a fixed-point equation, and a *deterministic equivalent* replaces the random resolvent by a deterministic matrix.

### Population covariance matrix

The observations are $y_j = C^{1/2} x_j$, where the $x_j$ are as in ch. 3 and $C$ is a deterministic positive semidefinite $N \times N$ matrix with bounded norm. The sample covariance is
$$
\hat C = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^n y_j y_j^* = \frac{1}{n}\, C^{1/2} X X^* C^{1/2} .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Deterministic equivalent for the sample covariance]{.tag} For $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$, let $\delta(z)$ be the unique solution in $\mathbb{C}^+$ of the fixed-point equation below, and $\bar Q(z)$ the matrix it defines:
$$
\delta(z) = \frac{1}{n} \mathrm{tr}\, C\, \bar Q(z), \qquad \bar Q(z) = \Big( \frac{C}{1 + \delta(z)} - z I_N \Big)^{-1} .
$$
Then $Q(z) = (\hat C - z)^{-1}$ is close to $\bar Q(z)$ in the following sense: for deterministic $A$ of bounded norm and unit vectors $a, b$, almost surely,
$$
\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, A\, \big(Q(z) - \bar Q(z)\big) \to 0, \qquad a^* \big(Q(z) - \bar Q(z)\big)\, b \to 0 .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch of the key step.* Write $Q_{-j}$ for the resolvent without the $j$-th sample. By Sherman–Morrison (Proposition 0.4),
$$
Q\, y_j = \frac{Q_{-j}\, y_j}{1 + \frac{1}{n} y_j^* Q_{-j}\, y_j} .
$$

-   $y_j$ is independent of $Q_{-j}$, so the trace lemma (Proposition 0.5) replaces $\frac{1}{n} y_j^* Q_{-j} y_j$ by $\frac{1}{n} \mathrm{tr}\, C Q_{-j}$.
-   Proposition 1.6 removes the index: $\frac{1}{n} \mathrm{tr}\, C Q_{-j} \approx \delta$, uniformly in $j$.
-   Then $I + z Q = Q \hat C = \frac{1}{n} \sum_j Q y_j y_j^*$, and taking expectations gives
    $$
    I + z\, \mathbb{E} Q \approx \frac{\mathbb{E}[Q]\, C}{1 + \delta} .
    $$

So $\mathbb{E}[Q]\, (\frac{C}{1 + \delta} - z) \approx I$. The error terms are controlled in Couillet and Liao (2022, ch. 2); for Gaussian data the method of ch. 3 applies verbatim. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $C = I$, $\bar Q = m I$ with $\delta = c m$, and the equation becomes the Marchenko–Pastur equation of Theorem 3.1. The word "equivalent" matters: when the spectrum of $C$ has no limit, $\bar Q$ has no limit either, but $Q - \bar Q$ still vanishes in the sense of the theorem.

When the ESD of $C$ converges to a law $H$, the limit is described by the companion transform. Let $\underline{m}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the limit ESD of the $n \times n$ matrix $\frac{1}{n} Y^* Y$, which has the same non-zero eigenvalues as $\hat C$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Silverstein's equation]{.tag} The limit ESD $F$ of $\hat C$ and its companion satisfy
$$
\underline{m}(z) = c\, m_F(z) - \frac{1 - c}{z}, \qquad z = -\frac{1}{\underline{m}} + c \int \frac{t\, H(dt)}{1 + t\, \underline{m}} .
$$
The second relation gives $z$ as an explicit function of $\underline m$.

::: proof
The deterministic equivalent of the co-resolvent $(\frac{1}{n} Y^* Y - z)^{-1}$ is $-\frac{1}{z(1 + \delta)} I_n$, so $\underline m = -1/(z(1 + \delta))$. Substitute $\frac{C}{1 + \delta} = -z \underline m\, C$ in the definition of $\delta$:
$$
\delta = -\frac{1}{z}\, \frac{1}{n} \mathrm{tr}\, C (I + \underline m\, C)^{-1} .
$$
Then replace $\delta$ by $-1/(z \underline m) - 1$ and pass to the limit. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is the equation of Marchenko and Pastur (1967) in the form of Silverstein and Bai (1995). Its explicit inverse gives the support.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — The support (Silverstein and Choi, 1995)]{.tag} On the real set where $\underline m \neq 0$ and $-1/\underline m$ is outside the support of $H$, define
$$
x(u) = -\frac{1}{u} + c \int \frac{t\, H(dt)}{1 + t u} .
$$
A real $x \neq 0$ lies outside the support of $F$ if and only if $x = x(u)$ for some $u$ with $x'(u) > 0$.

The edges of the support are therefore the values of $x(u)$ at the critical points $x'(u) = 0$.
::::

When $H$ has several atoms and $c$ is small, the support splits into clusters, one per population eigenvalue. Bai and Silverstein (1999) show that the sample eigenvalues then split exactly as the population ones do. This *separation condition* is what ch. 9 needs to estimate each population eigenvalue.

::: ex
[Example 4.4 — Two population eigenvalues]{.tag} Take $H = \frac{1}{2}\delta_1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta_4$ and $c = 0.1$. The critical points of $x(u)$ give the support
$$
[0.555,\ 1.408] \cup [2.485,\ 6.052] .
$$
The two clusters are separated, half of the sample eigenvalues lie below 2, and each cluster is wider than its population value: the eigenvalue 4 spreads over an interval of length 3.6.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
N, n = 1000, 10000                    # c = N/n = 0.1
c = N / n
t, w = np.array([1.0, 4.0]), np.array([0.5, 0.5])   # population spectrum H
pop = np.repeat(t, N // 2)

def det_equiv(z, iters=500):
    """Fixed point delta = (1/n) tr C (C/(1+delta) - z)^{-1}; returns (1/N) tr Qbar(z)."""
    delta = 1.0 + 0j
    for _ in range(iters):
        delta = 0.5 * delta + 0.5 * np.sum(pop / (pop / (1 + delta) - z)) / n
    return np.mean(1 / (pop / (1 + delta) - z))

def support_edges(c, t, w):
    """Edges of the limit support: x(u) = -1/u + c sum w t/(1+tu) is increasing off the support."""
    u = -np.logspace(-3, 3, 200000)
    x = -1 / u + c * np.sum(w * t / (1 + np.outer(u, t)), axis=1)
    dx = 1 / u**2 - c * np.sum(w * t**2 / (1 + np.outer(u, t)) ** 2, axis=1)
    flips = np.nonzero(np.diff(dx > 0))[0]
    return np.sort(x[flips])

Y = np.sqrt(pop)[:, None] * rng.standard_normal((N, n))   # columns ~ N(0, C)
lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Y @ Y.T / n)
for z in [0.5 + 0.1j, 2.0 + 0.1j, 4.0 + 0.1j]:
    print(f"z={z}: m_N(z) = {np.mean(1 / (lam - z)):.4f}, deterministic = {det_equiv(z):.4f}")
print("support edges (theory):", np.round(support_edges(c, t, w), 3))
print(f"sample eigenvalue range: [{lam.min():.3f}, {lam.max():.3f}], "
      f"fraction below 2: {np.mean(lam < 2):.3f}")
```

The empirical and deterministic Stieltjes transforms agree to $5 \times 10^{-4}$ at $z = 2 + 0.1i$, in the gap, and to within $10^{-2}$ inside the clusters, where $\Im z = 0.1$ resolves fewer eigenvalues. The sample eigenvalues range over $[0.552, 5.997]$, inside the predicted support up to the edge fluctuations of ch. 7.

### Variance profile

In a wireless channel or a bipartite network, each entry may have its own variance. Let $Y_{ij} = \frac{\sigma_{ij}}{\sqrt{n}} X_{ij}$ with bounded deterministic $\sigma_{ij}$ and standardized independent $X_{ij}$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Variance profile (Girko; Hachem, Loubaton and Najim, 2007)]{.tag} For $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$, the system below has a unique solution $(t_i(z))_{i \leq N}$, $(\tilde t_j(z))_{j \leq n}$ of Stieltjes transforms of probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^+$:
$$
t_i(z) = \frac{-1}{z \big(1 + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j} \sigma_{ij}^2\, \tilde t_j(z)\big)}, \qquad \tilde t_j(z) = \frac{-1}{z \big(1 + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i} \sigma_{ij}^2\, t_i(z)\big)} .
$$
Almost surely,
$$
\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\,(YY^* - z)^{-1} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_i t_i(z) \to 0 .
$$
::::

With $\sigma_{ij} = 1$, $t_i = m_c$ and $\tilde t_j = \underline m$: the system collapses to the Marchenko–Pastur equation. When $\sigma_{ij}^2 = d_i$ depends on the row only, it is the population model with $C = \mathrm{diag}(d_i)$ (Exercise 11). The proof follows the scheme of Theorem 3.1, with one equation per row and one per column; Hachem, Loubaton and Najim (2007) also give the deterministic equivalents of the mutual information used in ch. 5.

### Signal plus noise

In the information-plus-noise model, a deterministic signal matrix $A$ is observed in white noise:
$$
\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} (A + \sigma X)(A + \sigma X)^* .
$$
Its columns are not centred, so it is not a sample covariance matrix, but it is the right model for deterministic sources in ch. 8–10.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.6 — Information plus noise (Dozier and Silverstein, 2007)]{.tag} If the ESD of $\frac{1}{n} A A^*$ converges to $H$ and $N/n \to c$, then the ESD of $\Sigma$ converges almost surely to a law $F$ whose Stieltjes transform is the unique solution in $\mathbb{C}^+$ of
$$
m = \int \frac{H(dt)}{\dfrac{t}{1 + \sigma^2 c\, m} - (1 + \sigma^2 c\, m)\, z + \sigma^2 (1 - c)} .
$$
:::

With $A = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$ the equation is again the Marchenko–Pastur equation. The three models share one structure: a self-consistent equation for a few scalar functions, solved numerically by damped fixed-point iterations, as in `det_equiv` above.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Population covariance: $Q(z) \approx \bar Q(z) = (\frac{C}{1 + \delta} - z)^{-1}$ with $\delta = \frac{1}{n} \mathrm{tr}\, C \bar Q$; equivalently Silverstein's equation for $\underline m$.
-   The inverse map $x(\underline m)$ gives the support; the clusters separate when $c$ is small enough.
-   Variance profiles and signal-plus-noise matrices have their own fixed-point systems, all reducing to Marchenko–Pastur in the white case.
:::

## 5. Multi-antenna (MIMO) channels: mutual information and ergodic capacity {#ch5}

A link with $n$ transmit and $N$ receive antennas carries more information than a single-antenna link, and the question is how much more. The mutual information is a log-determinant of a random matrix, so its large-system limit is a functional of the spectra of ch. 3 and ch. 4.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — MIMO channel]{.tag} A narrow-band MIMO channel maps the transmitted vector $x \in \mathbb{C}^n$ to
$$
y = \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{n}}\, H x + w ,
$$
where $H$ is the $N \times n$ channel matrix, known to the receiver, $w \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, I_N)$ is the noise, and $\rho$ is the signal-to-noise ratio.

In the Rayleigh model, $H$ has independent $\mathcal{CN}(0, 1)$ entries; in the correlated model, $H = R^{1/2} X$ with a receive correlation matrix $R$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Mutual information with Gaussian input]{.tag} With $x \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, I_n)$ independent of $w$, the mutual information between $x$ and $y$, given $H$, is, in nats per channel use,
$$
I_N(\rho) = \log \det\Big( I_N + \frac{\rho}{n} H H^* \Big) = \sum_{k=1}^N \log\big(1 + \rho\, \lambda_k\big) ,
$$
where $\lambda_k$ are the eigenvalues of $\frac{1}{n} H H^*$.

::: proof
$I(x; y) = h(y) - h(y \mid x) = h(y) - h(w)$. Given $H$, $y$ is circular Gaussian with covariance $I_N + \frac{\rho}{n} H H^*$, and a circular Gaussian vector with covariance $K$ has entropy $\log \det(\pi e K)$. The difference is the log-determinant. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When the transmitter does not know $H$, Telatar (1999) shows that for Rayleigh fading the isotropic Gaussian input is optimal. The **ergodic capacity** is then the average $\mathbb{E}\, I_N(\rho)$ over the fading, the rate achievable by coding over many independent channel realizations.

### The large-system limit

By Proposition 5.2, $\frac{1}{N} I_N(\rho)$ is the integral of $\log(1 + \rho \lambda)$ against the ESD of $\frac{1}{n} HH^*$, and the integrand is unbounded only logarithmically. Theorem 3.1 therefore gives the limit of the capacity per receive antenna, and the deterministic equivalent gives it in closed form.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Deterministic equivalent of the mutual information]{.tag} Let $H = R^{1/2} X$, with $X$ standard complex Gaussian and the eigenvalues $r_1, \dots, r_N$ of $R$ bounded. Let $\delta > 0$ be the unique positive solution of
$$
\delta = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\rho\, r_i\, (1 + \delta)}{\rho\, r_i + 1 + \delta} ,
$$
and define the deterministic quantity
$$
\bar I_N(\rho) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log\Big(1 + \frac{\rho\, r_i}{1 + \delta}\Big) + n \log(1 + \delta) - \frac{n\, \delta}{1 + \delta} .
$$
Then $\mathbb{E}\, I_N(\rho) - \bar I_N(\rho) \to 0$, without normalization by $N$.

::: proof
*Sketch.* Write $s = 1/\rho$; then $I_N = \log\det(\hat C + s I) - N \log s$ with $\hat C = \frac{1}{n} H H^*$.

1.  *Derivative.* Differentiating in $s$,
    $$
    \frac{d}{ds} I_N = \mathrm{tr}\, (\hat C + s)^{-1} - \frac{N}{s} = \mathrm{tr}\, Q(-s) - \frac{N}{s} ,
    $$
    and Theorem 4.1 replaces $Q(-s)$ by $\bar Q(-s)$.
2.  *Envelope.* Define $\Phi(\delta, s) = \bar I_N$ as a function of both variables. A direct computation shows that $\partial \Phi / \partial \delta = 0$ exactly at the fixed point, and that $\partial \Phi / \partial s = \mathrm{tr}\, \bar Q(-s) - N/s$.
3.  *Integration.* Both sides tend to 0 as $s \to \infty$; integrating the derivatives from $s$ to $\infty$ gives the claim.

The rate $O(1/N)$ of the error is proved by Hachem, Khorunzhiy, Loubaton, Najim and Pastur (2008) with integration by parts and the Poincaré–Nash inequality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For $R = I$ and $c = N/n$ the limit per receive antenna is the Shannon transform of the Marchenko–Pastur law:
$$
\frac{1}{N}\, \bar I_N(\rho) = \log\Big(1 + \frac{\rho}{1 + \delta}\Big) + \frac{1}{c} \log(1 + \delta) - \frac{\delta}{c\, (1 + \delta)} = \int \log(1 + \rho \lambda)\, \mu_c(d\lambda) .
$$

::: key
[Key result — linear growth of the capacity]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}\, I_N(\rho) \approx N\, \mathcal{V}_c(\rho), \qquad \mathcal{V}_c(\rho) = \int \log(1 + \rho \lambda)\, \mu_c(d\lambda)
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — An 8 × 8 link at 10 dB]{.tag} For $N = n$ ($c = 1$) and $\rho = 10$, the fixed point is $\delta = 2.7016$, and
$$
\mathcal{V}_1(10) = 1.888 \text{ nats} = 2.72 \text{ bits per receive antenna} .
$$
An $8 \times 8$ link therefore carries about $21.8$ bits per channel use, against $2.9$ bits for a single Rayleigh antenna at the same total power: the capacity grows linearly in the number of antennas.
:::

Foschini and Gans (1998) and Telatar (1999) observed this linear growth; the closed form of the Shannon transform of $\mu_c$ appears in Verdú and Shamai (1999), for random spreading in CDMA.

At high SNR, $\mathcal{V}_c(\rho) \approx \min(1, 1/c) \log \rho$ up to a constant: the slope $\min(N, n)$ of $I_N$ in $\log \rho$ is the *multiplexing gain*. Receive correlation lowers the constant but not the slope as long as $R$ is invertible.

The code compares Monte Carlo averages with Theorem 5.3, for independent and correlated antennas ($R_{ij} = r^{|i - j|}$), down to $N = n = 2$:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)

def det_equiv_mi(R, n, rho, iters=500):
    """Deterministic equivalent of E log det(I + rho/n R^{1/2} X X^* R^{1/2}), in nats."""
    N, s2 = R.shape[0], 1 / rho
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(R)
    d = 1.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        d = 0.5 * d + 0.5 * np.sum(ev / (ev / (1 + d) + s2)) / n
    return (np.sum(np.log(1 + ev / (s2 * (1 + d))))
            + n * np.log(1 + d) - n * d / (1 + d))

def monte_carlo_mi(R, n, rho, reps=4000):
    N = R.shape[0]
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(R)
    out = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        X = (rng.standard_normal((N, n)) + 1j * rng.standard_normal((N, n))) / np.sqrt(2)
        H = L @ X
        out.append(np.linalg.slogdet(np.eye(N) + rho / n * H @ H.conj().T)[1])
    return np.mean(out), np.std(out)

rho = 10.0                                   # SNR of 10 dB
for N in [2, 4, 8]:
    for r in [0.0, 0.8]:                     # receive correlation R_ij = r^|i-j|
        R = r ** np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(N), np.arange(N)))
        mc, sd = monte_carlo_mi(R, N, rho)
        de = det_equiv_mi(R, N, rho)
        print(f"N=n={N}, r={r}: Monte Carlo {mc / np.log(2):6.3f} bits "
              f"(sd {sd / np.log(2):.2f}), deterministic equivalent {de / np.log(2):6.3f} bits")
```

Even for $N = n = 2$ the error is below 0.1 bit, and for $N = n = 8$ it is about 0.015 bit. The standard deviation of $I_N$ stays between 1.0 and 1.3 bits whatever $N$: the mutual information fluctuates by $O(1)$, as Proposition 2.4 suggests, and ch. 13 gives the Gaussian limit that predicts outage probabilities.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   With Gaussian input, the mutual information of a MIMO channel is $\log\det(I + \frac{\rho}{n} H H^*)$, a linear spectral statistic.
-   Its deterministic equivalent solves one scalar fixed-point equation, is accurate to $O(1/N)$, and shows a capacity growing linearly with the number of antennas.
-   Correlation between antennas lowers the capacity through the eigenvalues of $R$ only.
:::

## 6. Spiked models: outliers and eigenvectors {#ch6}

A low-rank signal does not change the limit spectrum (Proposition 1.6), but it can push a few eigenvalues out of the bulk. Whether it does depends on its strength, with a sharp threshold. This phase transition decides whether principal component analysis, detection or clustering can see a signal at all.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Spiked models]{.tag} Let $r$ be fixed, $\ell_1 > \dots > \ell_r > 0$ and $u_1, \dots, u_r$ orthonormal in $\mathbb{R}^N$.

-   *Spiked covariance* (Johnstone, 2001): the population covariance is $C = I_N + \sum_{k} \ell_k u_k u_k^\top$, and $\hat C = \frac{1}{n} C^{1/2} X X^\top C^{1/2}$.
-   *Spiked Wigner*: $W + \theta\, v v^\top$, with $W$ as in Theorem 2.5, $\theta > 0$ and $\|v\| = 1$.

The $\ell_k$ and $\theta$ are the *spikes*. Their eigenvectors are the signal to be recovered.
:::

The proofs reduce the location of an outlier to a scalar equation involving a quadratic form of the resolvent. The key input is that such forms behave like normalized traces.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Isotropic quadratic forms]{.tag} Let $\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X X^\top$ with Gaussian $X$, $u$ a deterministic unit vector, and $z$ at a fixed positive distance from $[a, b]$. Almost surely,
$$
u^\top Q(z)\, u - m_c(z) \to 0 .
$$
The same holds for $W$ of Theorem 2.5, with $m_{\mathrm{sc}}$ and $[-2, 2]$.

::: proof
For every orthogonal $O$, $O X$ has the law of $X$, so $O Q O^\top$ has the law of $Q$.

Hence $u^\top Q u$ has the law of $o^\top Q o$, with $o$ uniform on the sphere and independent of $Q$.

Write $o = g / \|g\|$ with $g \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_N)$. Conditionally on $Q$, Proposition 0.5 gives $\frac{1}{N} g^\top Q g - \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, Q \to 0$, and $\|g\|^2 / N \to 1$.

By Theorem 3.4 (and its Wigner analogue), $\|Q(z)\|$ stays bounded for $z$ away from $[a, b]$, so these bounds hold uniformly. Theorem 3.1 gives $\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, Q \to m_c$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### The spiked Wigner model

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Outlier and eigenvector of a spiked Wigner matrix]{.tag} Let $\hat\lambda$ and $\hat v$ be the top eigenvalue and a unit top eigenvector of $W + \theta v v^\top$. Almost surely:
$$
\hat\lambda \to \begin{cases} \theta + 1/\theta & \text{if } \theta > 1, \\ 2 & \text{if } \theta \leq 1, \end{cases} \qquad |\langle v, \hat v \rangle|^2 \to \begin{cases} 1 - 1/\theta^2 & \text{if } \theta > 1, \\ 0 & \text{if } \theta \leq 1. \end{cases}
$$

::: proof
Let $\lambda > 2$ be an eigenvalue of $W + \theta v v^\top$. By the Wigner analogue of Theorem 3.4 (ch. 13), it is not an eigenvalue of $W$ for large $N$. Let $R(\lambda) = (\lambda - W)^{-1}$.

1.  *Eigenvalue equation.* The determinant lemma gives
    $$
    \det(\lambda - W - \theta v v^\top) = \det(\lambda - W)\,\big(1 - \theta\, v^\top R(\lambda) v\big) ,
    $$
    so $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue iff $\theta\, v^\top R(\lambda)\, v = 1$.
2.  *Limit equation.* By Proposition 6.2, $v^\top R(\lambda) v \to -m_{\mathrm{sc}}(\lambda)$, which decreases from 1 to 0 on $(2, \infty)$. The equation $-m_{\mathrm{sc}}(\lambda) = 1/\theta$ has a solution iff $\theta > 1$.
3.  *Location.* Insert $m = -1/\theta$ in $m^2 + \lambda m + 1 = 0$: $\lambda = \theta + 1/\theta$.
4.  *Eigenvector.* From $(\lambda - W)\hat v = \theta \langle v, \hat v\rangle\, v$, $\hat v = \theta \langle v, \hat v \rangle\, R v$. Normalizing,
    $$
    |\langle v, \hat v \rangle|^2 = \frac{1}{\theta^2\, v^\top R^2 v} .
    $$
5.  *Derivative.* Since $R(\lambda)^2 = -\frac{d}{d\lambda} R(\lambda)$,
    $$
    v^\top R(\lambda)^2 v = -\frac{d}{d\lambda}\, v^\top R(\lambda) v \to m_{\mathrm{sc}}'(\lambda) .
    $$
    Differentiating $m^2 + \lambda m + 1 = 0$ at $m = -1/\theta$ gives $m_{\mathrm{sc}}' = 1/(\theta^2 - 1)$, hence the alignment $1 - 1/\theta^2$.

For $\theta \leq 1$ there is no outlier, the top eigenvalue sticks to the edge 2, and the eigenvector is asymptotically orthogonal to $v$ (Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi, 2011). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### The spiked covariance model

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.4 — Phase transition for sample covariance matrices]{.tag} In the spiked covariance model with $N/n \to c$, for each $k \leq r$, almost surely,
$$
\hat\lambda_k \to \begin{cases} (1 + \ell_k)\Big(1 + \dfrac{c}{\ell_k}\Big) & \text{if } \ell_k > \sqrt{c}, \\ (1 + \sqrt{c})^2 & \text{if } \ell_k \leq \sqrt{c}, \end{cases}
$$
and the $k$-th sample eigenvector $\hat u_k$ satisfies
$$
|\langle \hat u_k, u_k \rangle|^2 \to \zeta(\ell_k) = \frac{1 - c/\ell_k^2}{1 + c/\ell_k} \quad \text{if } \ell_k > \sqrt{c}, \qquad 0 \text{ otherwise} ,
$$
with $\langle \hat u_k, u_j \rangle \to 0$ for $j \neq k$. These results are due to Baik, Ben Arous and Péché (2005), Baik and Silverstein (2006) and Paul (2007).

::: proof
*Eigenvalues, for $r = 1$.* Write $\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X X^\top$ and $C = I + \ell u u^\top$. The matrix $\hat C$ has the eigenvalues of $\Sigma C$.

1.  For $\lambda$ not an eigenvalue of $\Sigma$, the determinant lemma gives
    $$
    \det(\Sigma C - \lambda) = \det(\Sigma - \lambda)\, \big(1 + \ell\, u^\top (\Sigma - \lambda)^{-1} \Sigma u\big) .
    $$
2.  With $(\Sigma - \lambda)^{-1}\Sigma = I + \lambda Q(\lambda)$, the outliers solve $1 + \ell\,\big(1 + \lambda\, u^\top Q(\lambda) u\big) = 0$.
3.  Proposition 6.2 replaces $u^\top Q u$ by $m_c(\lambda)$. The limit equation is $m_c(\lambda) = -\frac{1 + \ell}{\ell \lambda}$.
4.  Inserting it into the Marchenko–Pastur equation and simplifying gives $\lambda = (1 + \ell)(1 + c/\ell)$.
5.  This value is the correct branch of $m_c$, the one that tends to 0 at infinity, exactly when $\ell > \sqrt{c}$. The map $\ell \mapsto (1 + \ell)(1 + c/\ell)$ reaches its minimum $(1 + \sqrt c)^2 = b$ at $\ell = \sqrt{c}$.

*Eigenvectors.* The alignment follows from a contour integral of $u^\top (\hat C - z)^{-1} u$ around the outlier; see Paul (2007) for Gaussian data and Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi (2011) in general. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the BBP phase transition]{.tag}
$$
\ell > \sqrt{c} \iff \text{the spike creates an outlier at } (1 + \ell)(1 + c/\ell)
$$
:::

Two consequences matter for every application of the course.

-   Below the threshold, the top sample eigenvector carries asymptotically no information about $u$: no method based on it can estimate the signal direction.
-   Above it, the sample eigenvalue overestimates $1 + \ell$ and the eigenvector is only partly aligned. Both biases are known functions of $\ell$ and $c$, so they can be inverted.

The inversion is explicit: $\ell + c/\ell = \hat\lambda - 1 - c$, and the larger root is
$$
\hat\ell = \frac{(\hat\lambda - 1 - c) + \sqrt{(\hat\lambda - 1 - c)^2 - 4c}}{2} .
$$
Ch. 10 uses it to correct the MUSIC algorithm.

::: ex
[Example 6.5 — Numbers for c = 0.5]{.tag} The threshold is $\sqrt{0.5} = 0.707$.

-   $\ell = 2$: the outlier is at $3 \times 1.25 = 3.75$ instead of $1 + \ell = 3$, and $\zeta = 0.875 / 1.25 = 0.70$.
-   $\ell = 1$: the outlier is at $2 \times 1.5 = 3.0$, barely above the edge $2.914$, and $\zeta = 0.5/1.5 = 0.33$.
-   $\ell = 0.6$: no outlier. A spike that raises the variance by 60% in one direction is invisible to PCA with $n = 2N$ samples.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
N, n = 400, 800
c = N / n                                   # threshold sqrt(c) = 0.707
u = np.zeros(N); u[0] = 1.0                 # spike direction

print(" ell   lambda_max  theory   |<u,u_hat>|^2  theory")
for ell in [0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]:
    lam_max, align = [], []
    for _ in range(20):
        Y = rng.standard_normal((N, n))
        Y[0] *= np.sqrt(1 + ell)            # population covariance I + ell u u^T
        lam, vec = np.linalg.eigh(Y @ Y.T / n)
        lam_max.append(lam[-1]); align.append((vec[:, -1] @ u) ** 2)
    if ell > np.sqrt(c):
        th_l, th_a = (1 + ell) * (1 + c / ell), (1 - c / ell**2) / (1 + c / ell)
    else:
        th_l, th_a = (1 + np.sqrt(c)) ** 2, 0.0
    print(f"{ell:4.1f}   {np.mean(lam_max):9.3f}  {th_l:6.3f}   {np.mean(align):12.3f}  {th_a:6.3f}")
```

Above the threshold the averages match the limits within 0.07 for the eigenvalues and 0.02 for the alignments. Near it ($\ell = 0.6$ and $1.0$) the finite-size effects are visible: the alignment is 0.05 instead of 0 and 0.35 instead of 0.33, because the transition is smoothed over a window of width of order $N^{-1/3}$.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   A spike $\ell$ produces an outlier iff $\ell > \sqrt{c}$, at $(1 + \ell)(1 + c/\ell)$; the eigenvector alignment is $\frac{1 - c/\ell^2}{1 + c/\ell}$.
-   For a spiked Wigner matrix, the threshold is $\theta = 1$, the outlier $\theta + 1/\theta$, the alignment $1 - 1/\theta^2$.
-   Proof pattern: determinant lemma, isotropic quadratic form, scalar equation in the Stieltjes transform.
:::

## 7. The largest eigenvalue and the Tracy–Widom law {#ch7}

Tests and detectors compare the largest eigenvalue with a threshold, so they need its fluctuations, not only its limit. They are of order $n^{-2/3}$, much smaller than the $n^{-1/2}$ of classical statistics, and their law is the Tracy–Widom distribution.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Airy kernel and Tracy–Widom laws]{.tag} Let $\mathrm{Ai}$ be the Airy function, the solution of $y'' = x y$ that decays at $+\infty$. The Airy kernel is
$$
K_{\mathrm{Ai}}(x, y) = \frac{\mathrm{Ai}(x)\, \mathrm{Ai}'(y) - \mathrm{Ai}'(x)\, \mathrm{Ai}(y)}{x - y} .
$$
The Tracy–Widom law for complex matrices ($\beta = 2$) has distribution function given by a Fredholm determinant, or by the Hastings–McLeod solution $q$ of Painlevé II, $q'' = s q + 2 q^3$ with $q(s) \sim \mathrm{Ai}(s)$ at $+\infty$:
$$
F_2(s) = \det(I - K_{\mathrm{Ai}})_{L^2(s, \infty)} = \exp\Big( -\int_s^\infty (x - s)\, q(x)^2\, dx \Big) .
$$
For real matrices ($\beta = 1$),
$$
F_1(s) = \exp\Big( -\frac{1}{2} \int_s^\infty q(x)\, dx \Big)\, F_2(s)^{1/2} .
$$
:::

Tracy and Widom (1994, 1996) derived these laws for the Gaussian unitary and orthogonal ensembles. Their means are about $-1.77$ ($\beta = 2$) and $-1.21$ ($\beta = 1$), their standard deviations about $0.90$ and $1.27$: both are skewed to the left.

::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — Tracy–Widom limit for Wishart matrices (Johansson, 2000; Johnstone, 2001)]{.tag} Let $X$ be $N \times n$ with independent real $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ entries and $N/n \to c \in (0, \infty)$. With
$$
\mu_{Nn} = \big(\sqrt{n - 1} + \sqrt{N}\big)^2, \qquad \sigma_{Nn} = \big(\sqrt{n - 1} + \sqrt{N}\big) \Big( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n - 1}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \Big)^{1/3},
$$
the largest eigenvalue of $X X^\top$ satisfies
$$
\frac{\lambda_{\max}(X X^\top) - \mu_{Nn}}{\sigma_{Nn}} \xrightarrow{\ \mathcal{D}\ } F_1 .
$$
For complex Gaussian entries, the same holds with $n$ in place of $n - 1$ and $F_2$ in place of $F_1$ (Johansson, 2000).
:::

Since $\sigma_{Nn} / n$ is of order $n^{-2/3}$, the largest eigenvalue of $\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X X^\top$ is $(1 + \sqrt{c})^2 + O(n^{-2/3})$.

::: proof
*Structure of the proof, complex case.*

1.  *Joint density.* For $N \leq n$, the eigenvalues of the complex Wishart matrix $X X^*$ have the density, with respect to Lebesgue measure on $(0, \infty)^N$,
    $$
    p(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N) \propto \prod_{i < j} (\lambda_i - \lambda_j)^2 \prod_i \lambda_i^{n - N} e^{-\lambda_i} .
    $$
2.  *Determinantal structure.* Writing the Vandermonde product as a determinant of Laguerre polynomials, orthonormal for $\lambda^{n-N} e^{-\lambda}$, makes the eigenvalues a determinantal point process with a kernel $K_N$ of Christoffel–Darboux form.
3.  *Gap probability.* $\mathbb{P}(\lambda_{\max} \leq t)$ is the probability of no eigenvalue in $(t, \infty)$, that is $\det(I - K_N)_{L^2(t, \infty)}$.
4.  *Edge scaling.* Near $\mu_{Nn}$, the Plancherel–Rotach asymptotics of Laguerre polynomials show that, in trace norm on $(s, \infty)$,
    $$
    \sigma_{Nn}\, K_N\big(\mu_{Nn} + \sigma_{Nn} x,\ \mu_{Nn} + \sigma_{Nn} y\big) \to K_{\mathrm{Ai}}(x, y) .
    $$
    The Fredholm determinants converge.

The real case needs Pfaffians instead of determinants (Johnstone, 2001). [∎]{.qed}
:::

The limit is universal. Soshnikov (2002) proved it for symmetric sub-Gaussian entries when $n - N = O(N^{1/3})$, Péché (2009) removed this restriction, and Pillai and Yin (2014) treated general entries with enough moments. El Karoui (2007) extended it to complex data with a general population covariance, with centring and scaling computed from the equation of ch. 4.

In the spiked model of ch. 6, the transition also changes the fluctuations. For complex Gaussian data, Baik, Ben Arous and Péché (2005) showed that the top eigenvalue keeps Tracy–Widom fluctuations below the threshold, and has Gaussian fluctuations of order $n^{-1/2}$ above it.

### Computing the law

The Fredholm determinant is the practical route: Bornemann (2010) showed that a Gauss–Legendre discretization with a few dozen nodes gives the distribution function to near machine precision. For $\beta = 1$, the formula of Ferrari and Spohn (2005) writes
$$
F_1(s) = \det(I - B_s)_{L^2(0, \infty)}, \qquad B_s(x, y) = \frac{1}{2}\, \mathrm{Ai}\Big(\frac{x + y}{2} + s\Big) .
$$

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import airy

# Tracy-Widom (beta = 1) CDF by Nystrom discretization of a Fredholm determinant
# (Ferrari-Spohn formula F1(s) = det(I - B_s) on L^2(0, inf), B_s(x, y) = Ai((x+y)/2 + s)/2)
xg, wg = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(60)
L = 12.0                                     # truncate (0, inf) to (0, L)
x, w = L * (xg + 1) / 2, L * wg / 2

def F1(s):
    B = 0.5 * airy((x[:, None] + x[None, :]) / 2 + s)[0]
    sw = np.sqrt(w)
    return np.linalg.det(np.eye(len(x)) - sw[:, None] * B * sw[None, :])

s = np.linspace(-8, 6, 1401)
F = np.array([F1(t) for t in s])
dens = np.gradient(F, s)
mean = np.trapezoid(s * dens, s)
sd = np.sqrt(np.trapezoid((s - mean) ** 2 * dens, s))
q95 = s[np.searchsorted(F, 0.95)]
print(f"TW1: mean {mean:.3f}, sd {sd:.3f}, 95% quantile {q95:.3f}")

# Largest eigenvalue of real white Wishart matrices, Johnstone (2001) centring and scaling
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
N, n = 100, 400
mu = (np.sqrt(n - 1) + np.sqrt(N)) ** 2
sigma = (np.sqrt(n - 1) + np.sqrt(N)) * (1 / np.sqrt(n - 1) + 1 / np.sqrt(N)) ** (1 / 3)
stats = []
for _ in range(2000):
    X = rng.standard_normal((N, n))
    stats.append((np.linalg.eigvalsh(X @ X.T)[-1] - mu) / sigma)
stats = np.array(stats)
print(f"simulation N={N}, n={n}: mean {stats.mean():.3f}, sd {stats.std():.3f}, "
      f"P(stat > {q95:.2f}) = {np.mean(stats > q95):.3f}")
```

The computed law has mean $-1.206$, standard deviation $1.267$ and 95% quantile $0.980$.

For $N = 100$ and $n = 400$, the standardized simulated eigenvalue has mean $-1.29$ and standard deviation $1.21$, and exceeds $0.98$ in 4.1% of the runs: a test at nominal level 5% is slightly conservative at this size.

::: ex
[Example 7.3 — A threshold for N = 100, n = 400]{.tag} Here $\sqrt{399} = 19.975$, so
$$
\mu_{Nn} = 29.975^2 = 898.5, \qquad \sigma_{Nn} = 29.975 \times 0.15006^{1/3} = 15.93 .
$$
The 5% threshold for $\lambda_{\max}(X X^\top)$ is $898.5 + 0.98 \times 15.93 = 914.1$, that is $2.285$ for $\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)$, while the edge is $(1 + 0.5)^2 = 2.25$.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   The largest eigenvalue of a white Wishart matrix fluctuates on the scale $n^{-2/3}$ around the edge, with the Tracy–Widom law $F_1$ (real) or $F_2$ (complex).
-   The proof is determinantal: gap probability of a point process, Laguerre kernel, Airy kernel at the edge.
-   The law is computed by discretizing a Fredholm determinant: mean $-1.21$, standard deviation $1.27$, 95% quantile $0.98$ for $\beta = 1$.
:::

## 8. Source detection in high dimension and spectrum sensing {#ch8}

A cognitive radio may use a frequency band only when the licensed (primary) user is silent. It must decide, from $n$ samples received on $N$ antennas, whether a source is present. With $N$ and $n$ of the same order and an unknown noise level, the tests of ch. 6 and ch. 7 are the right tools.

### The test

Under the null hypothesis $\mathcal{H}_0$ the samples are noise; under $\mathcal{H}_1$ a single source with unknown channel $h \in \mathbb{C}^N$ is present:
$$
\mathcal{H}_0 : y_t = \sigma w_t, \qquad \mathcal{H}_1 : y_t = h\, s_t + \sigma w_t, \qquad t = 1, \dots, n ,
$$
with independent standard complex Gaussian $s_t$ and $w_t$, and unknown $\sigma^2$. The population covariance is $R = h h^* + \sigma^2 I$ under $\mathcal{H}_1$.

The signal-to-noise ratio is $\rho = \|h\|^2 / \sigma^2$, and the sample covariance is $\hat R = \frac{1}{n} \sum_t y_t y_t^*$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.1 — The generalized likelihood ratio test]{.tag} The generalized likelihood ratio, with $h$ and $\sigma^2$ replaced by their maximum likelihood estimates, is an increasing function of
$$
T_N = \frac{\lambda_{\max}(\hat R)}{\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, \hat R}
$$
on the range $1 < T_N < N$. The GLRT rejects $\mathcal{H}_0$ when $T_N$ exceeds a threshold.

::: proof
The likelihood of $n$ circular Gaussian samples is proportional to $\det(R)^{-n} \exp(-n\, \mathrm{tr}\, R^{-1} \hat R)$.

1.  *Under $\mathcal{H}_0$*, $R = \sigma^2 I$ and the maximum is reached at $\hat\sigma_0^2 = \frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, \hat R$, with value $(\hat\sigma_0^2)^{-Nn} e^{-Nn}$.
2.  *Under $\mathcal{H}_1$*, the maximum over $R = h h^* + \sigma^2 I$ (a classical computation, detailed by Bianchi et al., 2011) is reached with $\|h\|^2 + \sigma^2 = \hat\lambda_1$, the top eigenvalue, and $h$ along its eigenvector. The noise variance and the maximum value are then
    $$
    \hat\sigma_1^2 = \frac{\mathrm{tr}\, \hat R - \hat\lambda_1}{N - 1}, \qquad \max = \hat\lambda_1^{-n}\, (\hat\sigma_1^2)^{-(N-1)n}\, e^{-Nn} .
    $$
3.  *Ratio.* With $T = \hat\lambda_1 / \hat\sigma_0^2$, the $n$-th root of the ratio is
    $$
    L(T) = \frac{1}{T\, \big(1 - \frac{T - 1}{N - 1}\big)^{N-1}} .
    $$
    Its logarithmic derivative is $-\frac{1}{T} + \frac{N - 1}{N - T}$, positive when $T > 1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

$T_N$ is *pivotal*: multiplying the data by a constant does not change it, so its law under $\mathcal{H}_0$ does not depend on $\sigma^2$, and the threshold can be set without knowing the noise level.

:::: thm
[Theorem 8.2 — The GLRT in the high-dimensional regime (Bianchi, Debbah, Maïda and Najim, 2011)]{.tag} Let $N/n \to c$ and $\rho$ be fixed. Almost surely,
$$
T_N \to \begin{cases} (1 + \rho)\big(1 + \frac{c}{\rho}\big) & \text{under } \mathcal{H}_1 \text{ with } \rho > \sqrt{c}, \\ (1 + \sqrt{c})^2 & \text{under } \mathcal{H}_0, \text{ or } \mathcal{H}_1 \text{ with } \rho \leq \sqrt{c}. \end{cases}
$$
Under $\mathcal{H}_0$, the fluctuations of $T_N$ around $(1 + \sqrt{c_n})^2$ are of order $n^{-2/3}$ with the Tracy–Widom law $F_2$, the same as those of $\lambda_{\max}(\hat R)/\sigma^2$.

::: proof
By pivotality take $\sigma = 1$. Under $\mathcal{H}_1$, $R = I + \rho\, u u^*$ with $u = h/\|h\|$, a spiked model with $\ell = \rho$: Theorem 6.4 gives the limit of $\lambda_{\max}(\hat R)$.

The denominator satisfies $\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, \hat R \to 1$ under both hypotheses, since the spike adds only $\rho/N$.

Under $\mathcal{H}_0$, $\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, \hat R - 1$ is of order $1/N$, a sum of $Nn$ independent terms. It is negligible on the scale $n^{-2/3}$, so Theorem 7.2 applies to $T_N$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Three practical conclusions follow.

-   *Threshold.* For a false-alarm probability $\alpha$, reject when $T_N > \mu_{Nn}/n + q_{1-\alpha}\, \sigma_{Nn}/n$, with the Tracy–Widom quantile $q_{1-\alpha}$ (real data use $F_1$, as in the code below).
-   *Detectability.* A source with $\rho < \sqrt{c}$ is asymptotically undetectable by this test: its power tends to the level $\alpha$. With $N = 50$ antennas and $n = 100$ samples, the limit is $\rho = 0.707$, or $-1.5$ dB.
-   *Noise uncertainty.* The energy detector, which compares $\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, \hat R$ with a threshold computed from $\sigma^2$, is optimal when $\sigma^2$ is known. Under an error on $\sigma^2$, its false-alarm rate tends to 0 or 1: this fragility is behind the "SNR wall" of Tandra and Sahai (2008).

Other eigenvalue-based detectors use the ratio $\hat\lambda_{\max} / \hat\lambda_{\min}$, whose limit under $\mathcal{H}_0$ is $(1 + \sqrt{c})^2 / (1 - \sqrt{c})^2$ (Cardoso, Debbah, Bianchi and Najim, 2008; Zeng and Liang, 2009). Estimating the *number* of sources uses the same ingredients, one eigenvalue at a time (Nadakuditi and Edelman, 2008; Kritchman and Nadler, 2009).

The code compares the GLRT with an energy detector calibrated for $\sigma^2 = 1$, when the noise variance is exactly 1 and when it is 1.1, a 0.4 dB error:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
N, n = 50, 100                               # sensors, samples: c = 0.5
c = N / n
q95 = 0.98                                   # 95% quantile of TW1 (ch. 7)
mu = (np.sqrt(n - 1) + np.sqrt(N)) ** 2 / n
sig = (np.sqrt(n - 1) + np.sqrt(N)) * (1 / np.sqrt(n - 1) + 1 / np.sqrt(N)) ** (1 / 3) / n
thr_glrt = mu + q95 * sig                    # threshold on T = lambda_max / (tr R / N)
thr_energy = 1 + 1.645 * np.sqrt(2 / (N * n))  # energy test calibrated for sigma^2 = 1

def statistics(snr, noise_var=1.0):
    h = np.ones(N) * np.sqrt(snr * noise_var / N)          # ||h||^2 / sigma^2 = snr
    Y = np.outer(h, rng.standard_normal(n)) + np.sqrt(noise_var) * rng.standard_normal((N, n))
    R = Y @ Y.T / n
    return np.linalg.eigvalsh(R)[-1] / (np.trace(R) / N), np.trace(R) / N

for snr, nv in [(0.0, 1.0), (0.0, 1.1), (0.4, 1.0), (0.8, 1.0), (1.2, 1.0), (2.0, 1.0)]:
    T = np.array([statistics(snr, nv) for _ in range(1000)])
    print(f"snr={snr:.1f}, noise variance={nv}: P(GLRT detects) = {np.mean(T[:, 0] > thr_glrt):.3f}, "
          f"P(energy detects) = {np.mean(T[:, 1] > thr_energy):.3f}, mean T = {T[:, 0].mean():.3f}")
print(f"GLRT threshold {thr_glrt:.3f}; (1+sqrt c)^2 = {(1 + c**0.5)**2:.3f}; "
      f"detectability threshold sqrt(c) = {c**0.5:.3f}")
```

The GLRT keeps its false-alarm rate near 0.04 whether the noise variance is 1 or 1.1, while the energy detector jumps from 0.046 to 1.000. Below the threshold ($\rho = 0.4$) the GLRT detects in 5.6% of the runs, about its level. Above it, its power rises to 0.55 at $\rho = 1.2$ and 0.96 at $\rho = 2$, against 0.33 and 0.61 for the energy detector.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 8

-   The single-source GLRT with unknown noise level is a test on $T_N = \lambda_{\max} / \frac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}\, \hat R$, which does not depend on $\sigma^2$.
-   Its threshold comes from the Tracy–Widom law; a source is detectable asymptotically iff $\rho > \sqrt{c}$.
-   The energy detector is fragile: a small error on the noise level drives its false-alarm rate to 1.
:::

## 9. G-estimation, power estimation and positioning {#ch9}

The spectrum of $\hat C$ is a distorted image of the spectrum of $C$, and ch. 4 gives the distortion explicitly. G-estimation, introduced by Girko, inverts it: it builds estimators of population quantities that are consistent when $N$ and $n$ grow together. This chapter derives the main estimators and uses them to locate a transmitter from received powers.

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Consistency in the double limit]{.tag} Let $\theta_N$ be a functional of the population covariance $C$, such as $\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{tr}\, C^2$ or an eigenvalue of $C$.

An estimator $\hat\theta$ built from $\hat C$ is **$(N, n)$-consistent**, or a G-estimator, if
$$
\hat\theta - \theta_N \to 0 \quad \text{a.s. as } N, n \to \infty,\ N/n \to c \in (0, \infty) .
$$
